title: The dog-duty ascetic
hookLine: a man living like a dog asks his fate; deeds bear fruit like themselves

lines: PUNNA THE OX, SENIYA THE DOG.
WHERE WILL HE GO AFTER DEATH?
cards: In the Buddha's India, some ascetics took vows to live like animals, believing it would purify them and lead to heaven. Two such men come to the Buddha together. Punna has vowed to live like an ox.

Seniya, naked, has vowed to live like a dog: he eats only food thrown on the ground, and when he sits down near the Buddha he curls up like a dog. Punna asks a direct question: this man has kept the dog vow a long time.
Where will he go after death?

teach.b: This is the fifty-seventh discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the dog-duty ascetic. The Buddha refuses to answer. Enough, Punna, let it be.
Don't ask me that. Punna asks again, and again the Buddha declines. Only on the third request does he answer, and carefully.

teach.h: DOG HABIT, DOG MIND, AMONG DOGS
teach.b: If someone develops the dog habit fully, the dog mind, the dog manner, then after death, he says, they are reborn among dogs.
And if they hold the view that this will take them to heaven, that is a wrong view, and a wrong view leads to a bad destination. The same with the ox vow. Hearing this, Seniya weeps.
Not, he says, because of what the Buddha said, but because he has practiced this vow for so long. Then the Buddha teaches the principle beneath it. There are four kinds of action.
Dark action with dark results. Bright action with bright results. Mixed action with mixed results.

teach.h: FOUR KINDS OF ACTION, DARK TO BRIGHT
teach.b: And action that is neither dark nor bright, which leads to the end of action itself. Deeds bear fruit like themselves: a being is reborn according to what they have done; they become what they practice.
And the ending is gentle. Both men take refuge.
Seniya asks to go forth, trains, and in time, the text says, becomes one of the awakened. The man who practiced being a dog for so long practiced something else, and became that instead.
The hard answer and the hopeful ending are the same teaching: what you keep doing, you become.

how: Buddhist teaching on karma holds that intentional actions shape the one who does them, here and in future lives; some teachers use MN 57's four kinds of action to explain this, and stress that a person can change direction by practicing what is bright.

o: a dog, as in Seniya's long vow
an ox, as in Punna's ascetic vow
a monkey that copies what it sees

games.q: the four kinds of action — tap the pairs.
p: leads to the end of action

s: the Buddha answered Punna's question right away
he declined twice, and answered only on the third request.
Seniya wept because the Buddha's words were harsh
he said he wept because he had practiced the dog vow so long.
Seniya later went forth and became one of the awakened
the text says he trained and in time reached the goal.

games.q: you're the Buddha. a man asks where his friend, who has lived like a dog for years, will go after death. the answer is painful. what do you do the first time he asks?
o: decline: let it be, don't ask me that.
games.why: the Buddha declines twice. only when asked a third time does he answer, carefully, and then teaches the four kinds of action.

practice: Choose one thing you do almost every day, how you wake, how you answer the phone, how you speak to yourself in the mirror, and ask without blame: if I practiced this for ten more years, what would I become?
Let the answer come honestly. If it's good, rest in it; if not, picture one bright action to practice instead, and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Kukkura. Dog: the vow Seniya kept for so long, before he heard that deeds bear fruit like themselves, and practiced his way to awakening.

orig.note: Pali kukkura: dog. the discourse is the Kukkuravatika Sutta, the dog-duty ascetic.

carryVoice: Your line: you become the habit. Seniya shows that a habit can change. Day four hundred forty-nine.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 57, Kukkuravatika Sutta (the dog-duty ascetic)
